gaps.concept: Combined hormonal contraception is available as an oral pill, transdermal patch, or vaginal ring.
gaps.why_tested: A stem asks whether these delivery routes share the same estrogen-related risks.

gaps.concept: Estrogen increases hepatic clotting-factor synthesis, explaining the increased risk of venous thromboembolism.
gaps.why_tested: A patient develops a pulmonary embolism after starting a combined contraceptive; the question asks for the mechanism.

gaps.concept: Inherited thrombophilia, including factor V Leiden, makes estrogen-containing contraception unsafe.
gaps.why_tested: A patient with a known clotting disorder needs a contraceptive choice. [CDC](https://cdc.gov/contraception/hcp/usmec/combined-hormonal-contraceptives.html)

gaps.concept: Nausea, breast tenderness, and breakthrough bleeding are common adverse effects of combined hormonal contraception.
gaps.why_tested: A new pill user reports spotting and breast tenderness without signs of a serious complication.

gaps.concept: Progestin-only contraception is an option when estrogen is contraindicated, including during breastfeeding.
gaps.why_tested: A breastfeeding patient or one with migraine with aura needs a suitable method.

gaps.concept: Traditional progestin-only pills primarily alter cervical mucus; ovulation may continue, and late pills reduce protection.
gaps.why_tested: A patient becomes pregnant despite taking a progestin-only pill inconsistently. [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/contraception/hcp/usspr/progestin-only-pills.html)

gaps.concept: Levonorgestrel IUDs act mainly locally and commonly reduce menstrual bleeding or cause amenorrhea.
gaps.why_tested: A patient with heavy menses seeks contraception, or an IUD user develops scant periods. [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/contraception/hcp/usspr/intrauterine-contraception.html)

gaps.concept: Irregular bleeding or spotting is common with the etonogestrel implant and DMPA; amenorrhea may develop with DMPA.
gaps.why_tested: A progestin-method user presents with unpredictable bleeding or absent periods. [CDC](https://cdc.gov/contraception/hcp/usspr/injectables.html)

gaps.concept: Active pelvic inflammatory disease or gonococcal or chlamydial cervicitis precludes IUD insertion.
gaps.why_tested: A patient with purulent cervical discharge requests an IUD. [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/contraception/hcp/usspr/intrauterine-contraception.html)

gaps.concept: IUD insertion carries a small early risk of pelvic infection; expulsion or uterine perforation can cause missing strings.
gaps.why_tested: A patient develops pelvic pain or cannot feel IUD strings after insertion.

gaps.concept: Pregnancy with an IUD in place requires consideration of ectopic pregnancy, despite the IUD lowering overall pregnancy risk.
gaps.why_tested: An IUD user has a positive pregnancy test and unilateral pelvic pain. [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/contraception/hcp/usspr/intrauterine-contraception.html)

gaps.concept: Copper IUDs are contraindicated in Wilson disease.
gaps.why_tested: A patient with impaired copper excretion requests nonhormonal contraception. [FDA](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2024/018680s074lbl.pdf)

gaps.concept: Condoms reduce sexually transmitted infection transmission; hormonal methods and IUDs do not provide that protection.
gaps.why_tested: A patient using highly effective contraception asks about protection from HIV or other infections. [CDC](https://cdc.gov/contraception/hcp/usmec/summary-contraceptive.html)

gaps.concept: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception works best within 72 hours; ulipristal and copper IUD remain effective through five days.
gaps.why_tested: A patient presents four days after unprotected intercourse. [ACOG](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/practice-bulletin/articles/2015/09/emergency-contraception)

gaps.concept: Ulipristal can delay follicular rupture after the LH rise begins; levonorgestrel is most effective before that rise.
gaps.why_tested: A periovulatory patient needs oral emergency contraception. [ACOG](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/practice-bulletin/articles/2015/09/emergency-contraception)

gaps.concept: Starting hormonal contraception immediately after ulipristal can blunt its ovulation-delaying effect.
gaps.why_tested: A patient takes ulipristal and starts a progestin pill the next day. [CDC](https://cdc.gov/contraception/hcp/usspr/emergency-contraception.html)

gaps.concept: Oral emergency contraceptives prevent or delay ovulation; they do not terminate an established pregnancy.
gaps.why_tested: A question asks whether emergency contraception and medication abortion have the same effect. [ACOG](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/practice-bulletin/articles/2015/09/emergency-contraception)

gaps.concept: Mifepristone also antagonizes glucocorticoid receptors and is contraindicated with chronic adrenal failure or long-term corticosteroid use.
gaps.why_tested: A patient taking chronic glucocorticoids is considered for medication abortion. [FDA](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2023/020687Orig1s026lbl.pdf)

gaps.concept: Mifepristone–misoprostol does not treat ectopic pregnancy.
gaps.why_tested: Persistent pain after medication abortion reveals an extrauterine pregnancy. [FDA](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2023/020687Orig1s026lbl.pdf)

gaps.concept: Medication abortion commonly causes cramping and bleeding; misoprostol also causes nausea, diarrhea, fever, or chills.
gaps.why_tested: Symptoms begin after misoprostol, and the question asks for an expected drug effect. [FDA](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2023/020687Orig1s026lbl.pdf)

gaps.concept: Lactational amenorrhea provides contraception when breastfeeding is exclusive or nearly exclusive, menses have not returned, and delivery was under six months ago.
gaps.why_tested: A postpartum patient asks whether breastfeeding alone prevents ovulation. [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/contraception/hcp/usmec/lactational-amenorrhea-method.html)
